source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Fourteen LLMs with no retrieval were near or worse than coin-flip on questions asked after their cutoffs. The best, GPT-4-1106, trailed the human crowd by a wide margin.
numbers: Test set: binary questions from 5 platforms published after 1 Jun 2023. Random Brier .250. Best zero-shot or scratchpad LM .208 (GPT-4-1106-Preview). Human crowd .149. Only GPT-4 and Claude-2 series beat .25 by more than .02.
quote: None of the models are naturally good at forecasting.
limits: Single test period. The crowd is an aggregate, stronger than individual humans.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting gives a weak forecaster. Any forecasting mode in our agent needs retrieval and aggregation, not just a good prompt.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: A retrieval, reasoning and ensemble pipeline came close to the crowd. LM writes search queries, ranks and summarises news, several scratchpad prompts, a fine-tuned reasoner, trimmed-mean aggregation.
numbers: Brier .179 vs crowd .149 (diff .03); accuracy 71.5% vs 77.0%. Per platform: INFER .134 vs .104; Polymarket .193 vs .157; Manifold .247 vs .310 (LM better there, small N). RMS calibration error .42 vs crowd .38.
limits: Hyperparameters tuned on validation; test is forward in time. Binary questions only. Paleka 2025 warns about leakage in retrieval.
agent_relevance: The GJP recipe (gather, estimate several ways, aggregate with trimming) works for LMs but still loses to the crowd.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: Ablations: retrieval gives most of the gain; fine-tuning a small one; the reasoning prompt alone adds little.
numbers: No fine-tune and no retrieval: .206 (near baseline .208). No fine-tune with retrieval: .186. Full: .179. Fine-tuned GPT-3.5 in place of GPT-4: .182. Trimmed mean was best of 5 ensemble methods on validation.
limits: Differences of .003 to .007 are close to the standard errors (.002 to .003).
agent_relevance: Spend budget on evidence gathering and aggregation before prompt wording.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The LM beats the crowd when the crowd is unsure and loses when the crowd is sure. It hedges toward the middle.
numbers: Crowd in .3 to .7: LM Brier .199 vs crowd .246. Crowd within .05 of 0 or 1: LM accuracy 7% higher but Brier .04 worse. Better at early retrieval dates and with 5 or more relevant articles. A selective-submission rule made the system beat the crowd.
limits: Found on validation, then applied to test. Authors blame safety training for hedging.
agent_relevance: Mirrors the human superforecaster edge: confident, discriminating forecasts. Our agent should be allowed to commit to extreme probabilities when evidence is strong.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs, aggregated by median, was statistically indistinguishable from 925 human forecasters on 31 binary Metaculus questions. The wisdom-of-crowds effect repeats for models.
numbers: LLM crowd mean Brier .20 (SD .12) vs human crowd .19 (SD .19), p = .85. Better than the .25 no-information benchmark, p = .026. Equivalence bound 0.081 passed (p = .017 and .040). Model differences F(12,354)=2.64, p=.002.
limits: Only 31 questions over 3 months. Preregistered. Paleka 2025 notes possible piggybacking on human forecasts.
agent_relevance: Supports several runs or models averaged in code. Single-model errors are correlated (schema G4), so a model crowd is weaker than a human crowd.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Individual models ranged widely, and models showed an acquiescence (yes) bias.
numbers: Mean Brier: GPT-4 .15; GPT-4 with Bing .16; Bard .19; Falcon-180B .21; Claude 2 .21; Mistral-7B .24; Llama-2-70B .25; Coral .38. Human .19. Mean model forecast 57.35% (SD 20.93), median 60%, but just over 45% of questions resolved yes.
limits: Small question set; model cutoffs earlier than the questions.
agent_relevance: A yes-bias is a calibration defect the scaffold must correct, for example by checking the base rate of yes outcomes.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: Study 2: showing the human crowd median to GPT-4 and Claude 2 improved them, but plainly averaging human and machine forecasts was better still.
numbers: Accuracy gain of 17% to 28% from seeing the median human forecast. The simple human-machine average beat the informed-LLM update.
limits: Two models, same question set.
agent_relevance: Models use a given prior less well than simple averaging does. Prefer code-side averaging to asking the model to integrate (fits schema rule 1).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy
finding: LLM advice from a prompt built on the superforecaster commandments raised human accuracy. A deliberately biased, noisy assistant helped nearly as much.
numbers: N = 991, six questions, preregistered. Both assistants raised accuracy 24% to 28% vs a weaker control model giving no numeric advice. After dropping one outlier item: superforecasting assistant +41%, noisy assistant +29%. Mean difference vs control -0.27 (superforecasting) and -0.19 (noisy), p < .001.
limits: Control was a weaker chat model, not humans alone. At aggregate level only the noisy assistant beat the control. One outlier item.
agent_relevance: The gain may come from any second opinion, not the content of the superforecasting prompt. Do not read prompt text as a validated skill transfer.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Study 1: 38 prompts (superforecaster persona, base rates, premortem, self-critique and more) on four LLMs. Almost none changed accuracy beyond noise. Bayesian reasoning made it worse.
numbers: Linear mixed model, Benjamini-Hochberg corrected. Bayesian Reasoning coefficient +0.03 (worse), t=5.4, p<.001; Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.033, p<.001. All other prompts: adjusted p at least .77. Base Rate First -0.011 (not significant after correction). Chain of Thought -0.011. Superforecasting Persona (Short) -0.001, p=.93. Self-Consistency +0.009.
quote: small prompt modifications rarely boost forecasting accuracy beyond a minimal baseline
limits: Models: Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B; Study 2 added o1 and o1-mini. Effects are small on the Brier scale.
agent_relevance: Strong support for guardrail G1: forced extra reasoning steps (Bayesian, propose-evaluate) can hurt. A superforecaster persona gives nothing.

source: Schoenegger, Jones, Tetlock, Mellers (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Study 2 compound prompts and prompts from outside sources also gave negligible gains, including on reasoning models. Prompts differed in how far they pushed forecasts from the midpoint, which seems to explain the harmful ones.
numbers: Bayesian Reasoning produced the largest spread from 0.5 (table value 0.476 with SD 0.250 against 0.428 with SD 0.207 for Base Rate First). Study 2 mixed-effects gain for Bayesian reasoning remained positive (worse): 0.025, p=.005, adjusted p=.036.
limits: Column meaning in the PDF text table is partly ambiguous; treat the 0.476 and 0.428 pairing as approximate.
agent_relevance: Procedures that push forecasts to extremes without evidence are a failure mode. Enforce calibration in code.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: On 464 Metaculus questions, frontier LLMs beat a published crowd Brier number but lost significantly to a small group of experienced forecasters. The paper first called them superforecasters, then changed the word after a trademark notice.
numbers: o3 mean Brier .1352; o3-pro .1386; GPT-4.1 .1542; o4-mini .1589; DeepSeek-V3 .1798; Claude 3.6 Sonnet .1810; GPT-4o .1883. Experts on 41 held-out questions: mean Brier .1222, median .0196. Naive linear trend: LLMs reach expert level before May 2027. Reference crowd .149 (Halawi) and .121 (Karger).
limits: Brier values across question sets are not comparable. Experts answered only 41 held-out questions (about 31%).
agent_relevance: Experts are right and confident on most items (median Brier .02). Our agent's room is in middle-probability questions.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters
finding: Each model forecast five times and Brier was averaged. The prompt told the model it is a superforecaster. DeepSeek models refused 9 China-Taiwan items.
numbers: Averaging 5 predictions reduced outlier noise; o3 mean .1352 vs median .1362. 9 questions unanswered by the DeepSeek API.
limits: No ablation of the superforecaster persona. Schoenegger 2025 found no effect.
agent_relevance: Averaging repeated samples is cheap and safe.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities (ICLR 2025)
finding: Superforecasters beat the public and the best LLM on a live, leak-free benchmark. First paper comparing LLMs to actual superforecasters on shared questions.
numbers: 200-question subset. Overall Brier: superforecasters .096 (39 recruited, about 8 forecasts per question), public .121, best LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet .122; all p<.001. On dataset questions superforecasters .076, public .096, GPT-4o .130. Best LLM without the crowd forecast: .136. LLMs given market freeze values did best.
limits: Small superforecaster panel. Top LLM scores partly came from seeing the market price on market questions. Comparison limited to the human-answered 200 of 1,000 questions.
agent_relevance: A measured gap to the target class. Best LLM results lean on human market prices.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities (ICLR 2025)
finding: The authors projected parity with superforecasters from model strength trends.
numbers: Brier vs Chatbot Arena: y = 0.506 - 0.000298x (R2 .47); parity near Arena 1406 (bootstrap CI 1346 to 1633). Brier vs log compute: y = 0.844 - 0.01213x (R2 .41); parity near 6.49e26 FLOP (CI 9.69e25 to 8.65e28; r = -0.67, p=.046).
limits: About ten models, marginal significance, extrapolation.
agent_relevance: Do not plan on parity; test on live tournaments.

source: Forecasting Research Institute (2026) LLMs Are Closing the Gap on Human Superforecasters
finding: ForecastBench update: the best LLMs sit just behind superforecasters. A minimal tool-using xAI setup and a multi-stage ensemble pipeline tie for best non-human.
numbers: Grok 4.20 Preview (Oct 2025) difficulty-adjusted Brier .102; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024) .117; gap to superforecasters .017; improvement about .015 per year. xAI: 8 samples averaged with web and X search and Python. Cassi ensemble (o3 plus GPT-5, retrieval, market comparison) gains nearly .01 from crowd adjustment. Projected parity Nov 2026 (95% CI Jan 2026 to Nov 2027).
limits: Extrapolated from one year. Superforecaster sample and newest models share no questions, so scores are difficulty-adjusted, not head to head. Preview model.
agent_relevance: A simple recipe (tools, 8 samples, average) is already near the top. Pipeline gains of about .01 come mostly from shrinking toward a market price.

source: Forecasting Research Institute / Good Judgment commentary (2026) Brier Index update and skeptical view
finding: From search summaries only: the Brier Index switch moved projected parity to about May 2027 (CI April 2026 to May 2028). A Good Judgment piece argues the board measures the question type where AI has its largest advantage.
numbers: Superforecasters 70.6% vs best LLMs 67.9% on the Brier Index (gap 2.7 points); best LLM gain 2.4 points in one year.
limits: Not opened. Date discrepancies between posts left unresolved.
agent_relevance: Treat parity dates as uncertain; use as a monitoring variable.

source: Metaculus (2025) Q1 2025 AI Benchmark Results
finding: In Metaculus's quarterly bot tournament, the best-bot team lost head-to-head to 10 Pro forecasters. The best single bot would rank 11th behind all ten Pros.
numbers: 424 bot questions, 34 makers plus 11 template bots, 45 bots; 96 questions shared with Pros. Bot team vs Pros -17.7 (95% CI -28.3 to -7.0), p = .0007 one-sided. Earlier quarters -11.3 (Q3 2024) and -8.9 (Q4 2024). Top bot metac-o1 (o1 plus AskNews) placed 25th of 617 in the human Quarterly Cup; community prediction 3rd.
limits: Wide intervals; no clear trend. Bots weaker on multiple-choice (-37.5) than binary (-9.8) and numeric (-8.7). The URL slug says Q2 but the figures read are Q1 2025; read through a summary.
agent_relevance: Pros, the persistent superforecaster class, stay ahead of bots across quarters.

source: Metaculus (2025) Q1 2025 AI Benchmark Results
finding: Scaffolding with a weaker model could beat a plain template with the same model: a gpt-4o bot with a scaffold placed 8th, the plain gpt-4o template 44th.
numbers: twsummerbot average spot peer score 5.51 vs -5.53 for metac-gpt-4o. AskNews beat Exa and Perplexity, not significant.
limits: One bot; with many bots, a lucky one is likely.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can matter as much as a model upgrade, but one bot is thin evidence.

source: Metaculus analyses via LessWrong synthesis (2026) AI forecasting in 2026: what 11 analyses say
finding: Across the Metaculus analyses, Pros led bots every quarter, and the gap did not close.
numbers: Pro lead in head-to-head peer points: Q3 2024 11.3 (CI -21.8 to -0.7, p=.036, 113 questions); Q4 2024 8.9 (p=.079); Q1 2025 17.7 (p=.001); Q2 2025 20.03 (CI -28.63 to -11.41, p=.00001, 93 questions). FutureEval 2026: best model about 16 peer points behind Pros; naive extrapolation puts bots past Pros near June 2027.
limits: Secondary summary of Metaculus posts. Linear extrapolation.
agent_relevance: A four-quarter persistent human edge is a group-level persistence result.

source: Metaculus analyses via LessWrong synthesis (2026) AI forecasting in 2026: what 11 analyses say
finding: Survey of 39 bot makers: winning bots used more research, more aggregation and more calls. Multiple personas were called a mistake.
numbers: Top five scaffolded bots beat their plain baseline by 5 to 11 peer points per question. Winners averaged 1.75 research sources vs 1.00 (r=.42, p=.006); 86% of winners aggregated forecasts; 38% capped predictions; about 28 LLM calls vs 7 (p=.022); dev time r=.08. No search provider was significantly better, and the best one rotated each season.
limits: Survey, correlational, self-reported.
agent_relevance: Supports multi-source evidence plus plain aggregation. Matches schema G4: no persona voters.

source: Metaculus analyses via LessWrong synthesis (2026) AI forecasting in 2026: what 11 analyses say
finding: Failed replication: an automated prompt optimizer that gave large gains on old questions did not help live. Post-hoc recalibration did help.
numbers: Optimizer part 1: about 18 points on GPT-4.1-nano. Part 2 live Fall 2025: optimized prompt +2.76 per question vs baseline +4.71 (351 to 354 questions); null on n=278. Platt scaling: Brier gain .016 binary (p=.00052) and .005 multiple-choice (p=.000053). One bot ranked 9th (Fall 2025) then 10th (spring 2026).
limits: Secondary summary. A single bot's rank is anecdotal.
agent_relevance: Offline prompt gains may not persist live (a persistence failure for methods, not people). Cheap recalibration in code is the robust fix.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Forecasting Future World Events with Neural Networks (Autocast)
finding: Earlier machine baseline on questions from Metaculus, GJOpen and INFER: models were far below the human crowd.
numbers: Best ML model about 65% accuracy on binary questions vs 92% for the human crowd (50% random). Halawi 2024 cites 65.4% vs 92.8%, later 67.9% (Yan 2024).
limits: 2021-22 questions, T5-class models with retrieval.
agent_relevance: Shows the pre-2023 baseline; by 2024 accuracy was 71.5% on harder questions.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies?
finding: On a Google-internal prediction set, LLM designs failed to beat humans. Models guess low probabilities for most events, which looks like skill where most events do not happen.
numbers: Human Brier .1334 on validation. A weighted Brier that scores yes and no outcomes separately exposed a model bias toward low probabilities. Adding multiple personas or external news gave worse Brier than the baseline prompt.
limits: Internal dataset; exact per-method table values are not safely readable from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Report accuracy by outcome class to catch a low-probability bias. Personas hurt again.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: A tool-using ReAct agent (search plus Python simulation) matched the human crowd on two-week questions. Ensembling helped the agent but not base models.
numbers: RTF mean of 3: Brier .170 (73.9% accuracy); Halawi-style GPT-4o system .177; plain GPT-4o .210; Llama 3 .256; GPT-3.5 .261; GPT-4 .265. Ensemble of 3 agents .169 vs single .180; ensemble SD .092 vs base LMs .150. Calibration index .0129 vs .0194 for GPT-4o.
limits: Two-week horizon, small sets; human crowd .172 on filtered questions.
agent_relevance: An agent loop with a code tool already implements the GJP habit of updating on new evidence.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Schoenegger (2025) LLMs Can Teach Themselves to Better Predict the Future
finding: Ranking self-generated reasoning pairs by distance to the real outcome and training with DPO improved two 14B models by 7 to 10% in prediction accuracy.
numbers: 12,100 questions; Phi-4 14B and DeepSeek-R1 14B gained 7 to 10% vs base and vs a randomized-label control, reaching about GPT-4o level.
limits: Training, not a scaffold; needs resolved questions.
agent_relevance: Outcome feedback is the teacher. We do not train, but we can log outcomes for later checks.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future (TMLR)
finding: RL with a Brier reward trained a 14B model to match o1 and improved calibration.
numbers: 1,265-question hold-out. Seven-run ReMax ensemble Brier .190 (CI .178 to .203), ECE .062. Modified-GRPO .192, ECE .054. Gain over base -0.025; vs o1 -0.011; the market price remained better by .039 to .041. Polymarket simulation ROI over 10%.
limits: Market price stayed more accurate. ROI is simulated.
agent_relevance: Calibration came from the reward, not prompts. A scaffold cannot copy that but can add an offline Brier check.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Logical consistency (negation, paraphrase, conditional checks) tracks real Brier and can be tested instantly. But training for consistency did not improve accuracy.
numbers: Average violation vs Brier correlation 0.85 (frequentist metric) and 0.49 (arbitrage metric) in one plot, 0.92 and 0.69 in another; some checks above R 0.9, others near zero. ArbitrageForecaster improved the optimized checks but not held-out checks or Brier.
limits: Part of the correlation is that better models are both more consistent and more accurate.
agent_relevance: A code-run check (P(A) + P(not A) = 1) is a free quality signal and a G3-style held-out test.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping, Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in Evaluating Language Model Forecasters
finding: Many LLM-matches-human claims may be inflated by leakage. Date-restricted search returns future-shaped results; backtest question sets leak outcomes.
numbers: At least 3.8% of one dataset and at least 10% of another had leaked-resolution questions; cheap classifiers reached over 80% accuracy on some sets from question shortcuts; one dataset estimated over 90% affected. Also: piggybacking on human forecasts, benchmark gambling, skewed question mix, Brier overweights high-base-rate items.
limits: Position paper with examples, not a full re-evaluation.
agent_relevance: Test our agent on live or post-cutoff questions only; Halawi and Schoenegger parity claims carry this caveat.

source: Superforecasting persistence figures (Mellers et al. 2015; Tetlock and Gardner 2015) as summarised by AI Impacts
finding: The human persistence baseline: year-to-year accuracy correlated .65 and about 70% of superforecasters kept the status.
numbers: Correlation .65 and 70% retention (Superforecasting p.104); aggregated GJP beat control by over 60% and an intelligence-community market by 25 to 30%; structural model multiple correlation .64.
limits: Secondary summary; training effect lasted at least a year, no size given.
agent_relevance: No LLM study reports a person-style persistence correlation. Bot rank persistence is anecdotal, and offline prompt gains failed live.
